issues.item: Triggers: Children Present: Being around children
issues.explanation: For an adult male sexual assault survivor, 'being around children' is not impossible as a trigger, but in this profile it is hard to connect clinically to the rest of the selected items and formulation. The other triggers (related news, motorcycle noise) plausibly cue intrusive memory reactivation, and the memory items are all intrusion/emotion based. 'Being around children' implies a distinct trauma meaning or developmental context that is not reflected anywhere in Memory, Threat, Negative Appraisals, or Maladaptive Strategies. Given the formulation is dominated by Triggers ↔ Memory links, this trigger stands out as insufficiently supported by the accompanying memory content and is the one item most likely to be incoherent.

vignette: Kai had always loved the ocean views from his roofing jobs, but lately, he'd been avoiding them. It wasn't just the physical strain that worried him - ever since the assault, he'd become acutely sensitive to anything that made him feel like he was losing control. The smell of alcohol on a coworker's breath would send him into a tailspin, transporting him back to that night. He couldn't explain why, but the sound of motorcycles revving up in the distance also left him feeling jumpy and irritable. After the attack, Kai found himself fixating on news reports about similar crimes. The more he read, the more convinced he became that it could happen again - not just to him, but to his loved ones too. His wife, Leilani, noticed the change in him first: how he'd become withdrawn and preoccupied, always seeming to be "elsewhere." Kai tried to shake off these feelings by throwing himself into work, taking on extra jobs and working longer hours. Busyness became his coping mechanism - as long as he was physically exhausted, he couldn't think about it. But the memories lingered, refusing to be silenced. They felt more real than his ordinary memories, like they were seared into his brain. Sometimes, Kai would recall specific details - the sound of footsteps outside, the feeling of being pinned down - with perfect clarity. At other times, he'd be hit by waves of grief and emotion without any clear image or memory to anchor them. It was as if his mind had developed a hair-trigger response to certain sights, sounds, and smells. Leilani tried to get Kai to open up about what happened, but he found it hard to articulate the emotions swirling inside him. He knew that talking about it would only make things worse - it would bring back the memories, make them more vivid and overwhelming. Instead, Kai turned to control mechanisms: restricting his food intake gave him a fleeting sense of power over his life. The connection between these habits and his memories was a vicious cycle: the more he tried to avoid physical stress, the more his mind seemed to wander back to that night. The more he restricted his eating, the more he felt like he was losing control - which only made him want to exert even more control over his body. As Kai's avoidance behaviors took hold, they began to impact his daily life in tangible ways. He started turning down jobs on high-rise buildings or near bars, opting instead for lower-paying gigs with fewer physical demands. His relationships with friends and family suffered too: Leilani felt like she was losing her partner to a constant battle with anxiety and PTSD. It wasn't until Kai had a panic attack at work - triggered by the smell of beer on a coworker's breath - that he realized he needed help. The incident scared him into seeking therapy, but what he feared most was facing those memories head-on, reliving them in all their visceral intensity. What he hoped for, more than anything, was to break free from this cycle and start rebuilding his life, his relationships, and himself.
